item.title: When a stable absenteeism rate hides a turn for the worse
item.description:
You have probably seen this play out. The year closes, the absenteeism rate comes in the same as the year before, someone writes “stable” in the report and the topic drops off the agenda. It makes sense: if the number did not change, why spend time on it?

Because a number that stands still can be the sum of things moving in opposite directions.

In the Absenteeism Radar, a dashboard I built for a fictional company, the rate went from 3.772% in 2024 to 3.774% in 2025. A difference of two thousandths of a percentage point. If the report stopped there, the conclusion would be “nothing changed.” But quite a lot did.

Separate what managers control from what they do not

The first step is to split the rate into two parts:

  • short-term: absences of up to 15 days, such as unexcused absences, short doctor’s notes and late arrivals. This is the part that day-to-day line managers can influence;
  • long-term: absences of more than 15 days, which occupational health usually follows case by case.

Once you split it, “stable” falls apart. Short-term absence rose 0.055 percentage points (from 2.45% to 2.51%). Long-term absence fell by almost exactly as much, 0.052 points (from 1.32% to 1.27%). One canceled out the other.

Then look inside short-term absence

You can dig deeper still. In 2024 there was an infectious disease outbreak between February and May, which inflated short-term absences that year. In 2025 the outbreak did not come back, and that group of reasons fell 0.113 points.

In other words, short-term absence only avoided a bigger rise because the previous year had been unusual. Take infectious diseases out of the count and all other short-term absences rose 0.17 percentage points, an 8% increase.

To sum up what the “stable” number was hiding:

Component 2024 2025 Change
Total rate 3.77% 3.77% +0.002 pp
Long-term 1.32% 1.27% −0.052 pp
Short-term 2.45% 2.51% +0.055 pp
Short-term, infectious diseases only 0.435% 0.322% −0.113 pp
Short-term, all other reasons 2.02% 2.18% +0.17 pp (+8%)

The improvement came from factors management does not control: an epidemic that passed, and long-term absences, which swing widely with just a few cases. The deterioration was precisely in the part management does control.

What I would do about it

Two simple changes to how this gets reported:

  1. Use the short-term rate as a management KPI for line managers. It is the rate that responds to supervision, scheduling and onboarding of new hires.
  2. Never present the total rate on its own. Always break it down into short-term and long-term, ideally with the main groups of reasons alongside.

A word of caution

Breaking the rate down shows where the change comes from, not why it happened. Knowing that short-term absence rose 8% outside infectious diseases is the start of the investigation, not the end. In the Radar case, the next step showed that the rise was concentrated in two night-shift teams; but that is a topic for another post.

If you track absenteeism at your company, the exercise is worth it: take the rate for the last two years and split it into short-term and long-term. Your “stable” may be hiding something too.

The data in this post is fictional, generated for the Absenteeism Radar project. See the project
